Take-home Exercise 3: Geospatial Analytics for Urban Sustainability

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code

A Huff model of morning boardings at Singapore’s MRT and LRT stations, and what the Jurong Region Line and Cross Island Line will do to them

Probabilistic spatial interaction modelling of station-level ridership: a Huff model calibrated on LTA passenger volumes and HDB dwelling units, used to predict boardings at the planned JRL and CRL phase 1 stations and their effect on the stations already open.

Author
Affiliation

Jedidiah Asaf Tallulembang

ISSS626 Geospatial Analytics and Applications

Published

November 14, 2026

Abstract

I model where Singapore’s HDB residents board the train in the weekday morning peak. A Huff model allocates the 1.18 million dwelling units of 10,817 HDB blocks to the stations around them, in proportion to each station’s attractiveness and inversely to a power of distance, and is calibrated against three months of LTA tap-in counts (August to October 2026).

The textbook Huff model, with every station equally attractive and a distance exponent of -2, explains 41% of the variation in log boardings across 148 stations with an HDB catchment. Letting attractiveness depend on the number of lines a station serves, the points of interest around it and whether it is LRT-only raises that to 75% out of sample, and ranks stations with a Spearman correlation of 0.90. A second line multiplies a station’s pull by about 2.6, more than a forty-fold increase in the shops and services around it would, and an LRT-only station has about one eighteenth of the pull of an equivalent MRT station.

Applied to the 2030 network, the model predicts that the Jurong Region Line will take the largest morning catchments in the network’s newest towns: Tengah Plantation, Choa Chu Kang West and the Jurong West stations, together drawing riders from Chinese Garden, Lakeside, Pioneer and Bukit Batok, whose morning boardings fall by 40% to 65%. On the Cross Island Line, Serangoon North and Pasir Ris East are the strong stations. Aviation Park, Jurong Pier, Jurong Hill and Loyang have almost no homes around them: under a home-based model they are the stations at risk of Hume’s decade in the dark, and their case rests on the jobs and development planned around them, which this model cannot see.

As a value-added analysis I let the distance decay differ by region, a geographically varying Huff model. Residents of the North-East and West are about twice as sensitive to distance as those of the Central region (exponents near -4 against -1.8), and the regional model predicts held-out stations better (R² 0.77 against 0.75). Re-running the 2030 scenario with it leaves the ranking of the new stations almost unchanged (rank correlation 0.95) but deepens the losses at Jurong East and Boon Lay, whose western residents abandon them more readily for a nearer JRL station.

Executive summary · Repository

1 Introduction and study context

Singapore’s rail network is planned decades ahead of the people who will ride it. The Land Transport Authority builds stations as shells where housing is expected, and opens them when the riders arrive. Sometimes they arrive late. Hume station on the Downtown Line had its structure finished in 2015 and opened on 28 February 2025, a decade later. Buangkok and Woodleigh stayed dark when the North East Line opened in 2003, because the operator judged that the riders around them would not cover the cost of stopping there. Several shells are still dark today: the station layer LTA publishes in September 2026 contains platforms at Bukit Brown, Mount Pleasant, Marina South and Founders’ Memorial that carry no passengers at all (section 4.2).

Two lines now under construction add more than thirty stations by 2030: the Jurong Region Line (JRL) in the west, serving Tengah, Jurong West and the Jurong Innovation District, and phase 1 of the Cross Island Line (CRL) from Aviation Park to Bright Hill. The questions a planner would ask are the ones this exercise asks: how many people will board at each new station, and which existing stations will lose riders to them.

These are questions about catchments, and a catchment is a probabilistic thing. A block of flats between two stations does not belong to either; some of its residents walk to one and some to the other, in proportions that depend on how far each station is and how much each offers. That is precisely what a Huff model describes, and why I use one.

2 Research question and objectives

Where do HDB residents board the train in the morning peak, and how will the Jurong Region Line and the Cross Island Line phase 1 redistribute them?

  1. Calibrate a probabilistic spatial interaction (Huff) model that estimates station-level morning boardings from where people live, how far each station is, and what each station offers, and test it against simpler reference models.
  2. Use it to predict morning boardings at the planned JRL and CRL phase 1 stations, with uncertainty.
  3. Show how the new stations change the boardings and market areas of the stations already open.

3 Data and study design

3.1 What is modelled

The brief asks for station-level ridership. I model one specific part of it: tap-ins on weekday mornings between 6:00 and 9:00, averaged over August, September and October 2026. The choice is deliberate. A Huff model of station catchments needs the riders it allocates to come from the places it allocates them from. In the morning peak most trips begin at home, so a station’s boardings are drawn from the housing around it. Over the whole day that stops being true: a station in the central area boards thousands of people in the evening who live nowhere near it. Figure 1 shows the difference in the data itself.

The local market potential of each origin is the number of HDB dwelling units in it. HDB flats house about four in five Singapore residents, and they are the only housing for which a public, block-level count exists. Private housing is the main omission, and it decides which stations the model can be judged on (section 4.3).

3.2 Data sources

The brief recommends the origin-destination version of the passenger data. On the day I ran the analysis DataMall refused that endpoint for my key with a quota violation, while the station-level endpoint answered normally. For a model of where people board, station-level tap-ins are all that is needed: the destination half of each trip plays no part in it. LTA’s bus stop file likewise could not be fetched by script, and OpenStreetMap supplies 5,668 bus stops in its place.

code 
d <- ex |> st_drop_geometry() |> mutate(in_fit = du_1km >= CAL_MIN_DU_1KM)
lab <- d |> filter(name %in% c("Yishun", "Woodlands", "Tampines", "Raffles Place", "Tanjong Pagar",
                               "Newton", "Kranji", "Changi Airport", "Tuas Link", "Punggol", "Jurong East", "Downtown"))
ggplot(d, aes(tapout_am, tap_am)) +
  geom_abline(colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.3, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = in_fit), size = 1.8, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(data = lab, aes(label = name), size = 2.8, colour = PAL$ink, seed = 1, min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) + scale_y_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = PAL$accent, `FALSE` = PAL$loss_lt),
                      labels = c(`TRUE` = "HDB catchment, in the fit", `FALSE` = "Little or no HDB housing within 1 km"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Tap-outs, weekday 06:00 to 09:00, per month", y = "Tap-ins, per month",
       caption = "LTA DataMall, Passenger Volume by Train Stations, mean of Aug, Sep and Oct 2026.") +
  theme_ex03(grid = "both")

4 Data preparation and quality assessment

4.1 Placing every HDB block

The dwelling-unit counts and the building footprints come in two files that share no key. The property file names a block by number and abbreviated street (“1 BEDOK STH AVE 1”); the footprint file by number and a street code (“BEA09N”) and postal code. Matching on block number alone is wrong, because block numbers repeat across streets and towns. The street code turns out to be one code per street (657 street names, 660 codes), so geocoding one block per street with the OneMap search API, and matching the returned postal code to a footprint, gives a complete street-to-code crosswalk (R/01_street_codes.R). That joins 10,734 of the 10,817 residential blocks. The other 83, mostly new blocks in Tengah built after the footprint file was last updated, were geocoded one by one and kept as points. Every residential block, and all 1,179,156 dwelling units, is placed. Each block’s origin point is a point on the surface of its footprint (st_point_on_surface(), in SVY21, EPSG:3414), which unlike a centroid always falls inside an L-shaped or U-shaped block.

code 
s_all <- lines_sf(stations)
ggplot() + base_land(subzone) +
  geom_sf(data = origins, aes(size = du), colour = PAL$muted, alpha = 0.25, stroke = 0) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(s_all, kind == "Existing"), shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = PAL$ink, size = 1.1, stroke = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(s_all, kind != "Existing"), aes(fill = kind), shape = 21, colour = "white", size = 2.3, stroke = 0.4) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 1.6, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Jurong Region Line" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], "Cross Island Line" = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(caption = "HDB Property Information and Existing Building (data.gov.sg); station coordinates from URA via data.gov.sg.") +
  sg_crop(stations) + theme_map()

4.2 Stations: what the passenger data says exists

A station appears in this analysis as a complex: Jurong East is one place to a resident walking from home, whether it serves one line or three. Codes were grouped by station name, giving 184 existing complexes and 30 new ones (22 on the JRL, 8 on the CRL phase 1). Seven existing stations gain a line in 2030 (Ang Mo Kio, Boon Lay, Bright Hill, Choa Chu Kang, Hougang, Jurong East and Pasir Ris), and the model counts their extra line only in the 2030 run.

The passenger data, not any station list, decides what operates. Three mines had to be cleared here:

  • Stations listed as planned that are already open. Keppel, Cantonment and Prince Edward Road, Circle Line stage 6, appear in the station list as future stations but carry passengers in all three months. They are moved to the existing network, as are the new Circle Line codes at Marina Bay (CC33) and Bayfront (CC34).
  • Stations that are built but not open. LTA’s own September 2026 station layer contains platform polygons for Bukit Brown (CC18), Mount Pleasant (TE10), Marina South (TE21) and Founders’ Memorial (TE22A), and a dozen depots, none of which board a single passenger. Taking that layer as the network would have added the very ghost stations the brief describes.
  • Joint codes. The passenger data codes an interchange once (“NS27/CC33/TE20”), so each data code is mapped to the complex of whichever of its parts the station list knows.

Morning boardings are stable from month to month: the correlation of log tap-ins between August and October is 0.993. Averaging the three months removes the effect of any single month’s disruption without hiding real differences.

4.3 Which stations the model can be judged on

36 existing stations have fewer than 1,000 HDB dwelling units within 1 km. Some serve private estates (Newton, Stevens, Sixth Avenue, Siglap, Hillview), some industry (Tuas, Joo Koon) or the airport, some the central area. Newton and Kranji each board more than 200,000 people a month in the morning peak with no HDB block within a kilometre. A model whose market potential is HDB flats cannot explain them, and fitting to them would bend every parameter towards explaining riders it has no data on.

So the rule (set in R/00_config.R) is that these stations stay in every block’s choice set, where they compete for HDB riders like any other station, but their observed boardings do not enter the fit. Figure 1 supports the rule from the data: the 148 fitted stations board 1.31 morning tap-ins for every tap-out; the excluded ones only 0.43.

4.4 Attraction variables

Each station’s attractiveness is measured within 400 m of it, about a five-minute walk:

  • Lines served today (and in 2030 for the scenario). A second line multiplies the destinations reachable without a transfer.
  • Bus stops, as a measure of feeder connectivity.
  • Points of interest: shops, food outlets, offices, schools, clinics and civic amenities in OpenStreetMap. Mapped areas (many malls and schools are drawn as outlines) are reduced to a point on their surface.
  • LRT-only: whether the station is served only by a light rail loop, from which most journeys continue by transferring to the MRT.

Counts enter as log(1 + count), so their exponents read as elasticities.

5 Methods and analytical decisions

5.1 The Huff model

The probability that a resident of block \(i\) boards at station \(j\) is

\[ P_{ij} = \frac{A_j \, d_{ij}^{\lambda}}{\sum_{l \in C_i} A_l \, d_{il}^{\lambda}}, \qquad A_j = \exp\Big(\sum_m \gamma_m x_{jm}\Big) \]

where \(d_{ij}\) is the straight-line distance from the block to the station, \(C_i\) is the block’s choice set and \(A_j\) is the station’s attractiveness, multiplicative in its characteristics \(x_{jm}\) as in an MCI model. The predicted boardings at station \(j\) are the dwelling units allocated to it, scaled by one trip rate \(k\):

\[ \hat T_j = k \sum_i DU_i \, P_{ij} \]

Three decisions shape it.

Choice set. A block chooses among the stations within 3 km, and always among its three nearest, so that blocks far from the network (Tengah has no station today) still choose. 3 km covers a walk and a short feeder-bus ride; it gives a median of ten candidate stations per block.

Distance floor. Distances under 100 m are set to 100 m, so that a block beside a station does not receive an effectively infinite pull under a power decay.

Calibration. The parameters (\(\lambda\) and the \(\gamma_m\)) minimise the mean squared error of log boardings across the fitted stations, with \(k\) solved in closed form. Boardings range from under a thousand to over 400,000 a month, and on the log scale a 20% miss costs the same at a small station as at a large one. Because the utility is linear in the parameters, the Huff model is a conditional logit over stations and the loss has an exact gradient (R/huff_core.R), which makes a 200-draw bootstrap practical.

The shares are checked against MCI::huff.shares() for one block: they agree to the 15th decimal place (largest difference 1.7e-16), which is floating-point noise. The MCI function needs every origin to share one set of stations, which is why the fitting uses a vectorised version; MCI is the reference it is checked against.

5.2 Reference models and validation

The rubric asks for reference and null models, and they are the only way to know whether the attraction terms earn their place. Four nested models are compared:

Each is scored by 10-fold cross-validation over stations: a tenth of the stations have their boardings hidden, the model is fitted on the rest, and the hidden stations are predicted. The hidden stations stay in every choice set. This is exactly the position of a new station, whose location and attributes are known and whose ridership is not, so the cross-validated error is the honest estimate of how well the model will predict the JRL and CRL stations.

6 Calibration results

6.1 Attraction matters more than distance

code 
bind_rows(cal$insample |> mutate(score = "In-sample"), cal$cv |> mutate(score = "Cross-validated")) |>
  select(model, score, R2_log, RMSLE, MdAPE_pct, spearman) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = score, values_from = c(R2_log, RMSLE, MdAPE_pct, spearman)) |>
  transmute(Model = model,
            `R² in-sample` = round(`R2_log_In-sample`, 3), `R² cross-validated` = round(`R2_log_Cross-validated`, 3),
            `RMSLE (CV)` = round(`RMSLE_Cross-validated`, 3), `MdAPE % (CV)` = round(`MdAPE_pct_Cross-validated`, 1),
            `Spearman (CV)` = round(`spearman_Cross-validated`, 3)) |>
  kable()

The textbook model already explains 41% of the variation in log boardings: where the housing is accounts for a good deal. Fitting the distance exponent alone adds nothing (-1.94 against the default -2). Adding the number of lines lifts the cross-validated R² to 53%, and the full model to 75%, with a median miss of 34% and a rank correlation of 0.9. The cross-validated scores sit close to the in-sample ones, so the extra terms are not fitting noise.

code 
lab_terms <- c(lambda = "Distance exponent (lambda)", n_lines = "Lines served", bus_stops = "Bus stops within 400 m",
               poi = "Points of interest within 400 m", lrt_only = "LRT-only station")
p <- tibble(term = names(th), estimate = th) |> left_join(cal$ci, by = "term") |>
  mutate(term = factor(lab_terms[term], rev(lab_terms)))
ggplot(p, aes(estimate, term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL$accent, size = 2.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", estimate)), vjust = -0.9, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink) +
  labs(x = "Estimate (exponent on log(1 + count); coefficient on the LRT indicator)", y = NULL) +
  theme_ex03(grid = "x")

Read as elasticities, the estimates say four things.

  • Distance decays steeply. \(\lambda\) = -2.48 (-3.24 to -1.82): doubling the distance to a station cuts its pull by a factor of 5.6, once its attractions are accounted for. The textbook -2 is inside the interval, but with the attractions in the model the data prefer a slightly steeper decay.
  • Lines served is the strongest attraction. Going from one line to two multiplies a station’s pull by 2.6. People walk further to an interchange because it saves them a transfer later.
  • Activity around the station adds a smaller pull. Ten times the points of interest multiplies attractiveness by 1.76.
  • LRT-only stations draw far fewer boardings. An LRT-only station has 6% of the attractiveness of an MRT station with the same attributes. Much of that is how LRT riders appear in the data: a Punggol resident who boards the LRT and transfers to the North East Line taps in once.

Bus stops, once the other terms are in, are not distinguishable from zero (the interval spans zero). Feeder connectivity is real, but around stations it moves with lines and activity, which carry the information.

6.2 Where the model misses

code 
d <- st_drop_geometry(stn)[cal$cal_idx, ] |> mutate(cv = cal$cv_pred[[cal$best]][cal$cal_idx], err = log(tap_am / cv))
lab <- d |> slice_max(abs(err), n = 10)
ggplot(d, aes(cv, tap_am)) +
  geom_abline(colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.3, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = lrt_only), size = 1.9, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(data = lab, aes(label = name), size = 2.8, colour = PAL$ink, seed = 2, min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) + scale_y_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = PAL$accent, `TRUE` = LINE_COLS[["LRT"]]),
                      labels = c(`FALSE` = "MRT", `TRUE` = "LRT only"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Predicted (held out in cross-validation), per month", y = "Observed tap-ins, weekday 06:00 to 09:00, per month") +
  theme_ex03(grid = "both")
code 
d <- stn[cal$cal_idx, ]
ggplot() + base_land(subzone) +
  geom_sf(data = d, aes(fill = pmax(pmin(resid_log, 1.2), -1.2)), shape = 21, size = 2.4, colour = "white", stroke = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$div, limits = c(-1.2, 1.2), name = "log(observed / predicted)") +
  sg_crop(stations) + theme_map()

The residuals are not random in space: Moran’s I is 0.16 (p 8.5e-05) with six nearest neighbours. The largest under-predictions are city-fringe stations whose catchments mix HDB blocks with condominiums and landed housing: Novena, Great World, Katong Park, Fort Canning, Beauty World, Aljunied. Their extra boardings come from residents the model cannot see. The largest over-predictions are of two kinds: stations that opened recently, where habits have not caught up (Keppel, in service only since 2026, and the small Punggol LRT stop at Teck Lee), and stations whose HDB blocks mostly walk to a stronger neighbour, such as Bendemeer, Labrador Park and one-north. Both patterns are regional, which is what Moran’s I picks up. Private housing cannot be added from the data available, but a single distance exponent for the whole island is a testable suspect, and section 8 tests it.

7 Predicting the 2030 network

The calibrated model is run twice on the same 10,817 blocks: on today’s stations and on the 2030 set, in which the 30 new stations exist and seven interchanges count their extra line. Comparing two runs of the same model isolates the effect of the new stations; comparing a prediction with observed ridership would mix that effect with the model’s own error. The intervals come from re-running the 200 bootstrap draws of the parameters through both networks.

7.1 Ridership at the new stations

code 
q <- quantile(stn$tap_am[cal$cal_idx], c(0.1, 0.5))
d <- res |> filter(new) |> mutate(name = reorder(name, pred_2030),
                                 line = ifelse(line_new == "JRL", "Jurong Region Line", "Cross Island Line"))
ggplot(d, aes(pred_2030, name)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = q[1], xmax = q[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = PAL$land, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = pred_2030_lo, xmax = pred_2030_hi, colour = line), height = 0, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = line), size = 2.2) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Jurong Region Line" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], "Cross Island Line" = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Predicted boardings per month, weekday 06:00 to 09:00 (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_ex03(grid = "x")

The strongest new stations are those planted in dense housing with no station of its own today. Tengah Plantation (178,800 a month) is the clearest case: Tengah’s 16,318 dwelling units currently have to reach Bukit Batok or Choa Chu Kang. On the CRL, Serangoon North (172,200) and Pasir Ris East (116,100) serve large estates that sit between today’s lines.

8 new stations fall below the 10th percentile of today’s stations: Tukang, Nanyang Gateway, Peng Kang Hill, Forest Hill, Loyang, Jurong Hill, Jurong Pier, Aviation Park. Most are in the Jurong Innovation District, at the airport or on the edge of Tengah, where there are few or no homes. In a home-based morning model they are exactly what the brief calls the ghost-station risk. Two cautions apply. First, their case does not rest on boardings at all: they are destinations, built for the jobs, campuses and terminal that will arrive, and their morning ridership will show up as tap-outs, which this model does not predict. Second, some are in towns still under construction (Tengah, Forest Hill), where today’s points of interest and bus stops understate what the station will offer in 2030.

7.2 What the new stations take from the existing ones

code 
d <- stations |> select(name) |> left_join(res, by = "name")
ggplot() + base_land(subzone) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(d, existing, !is.na(change_pct)),
          aes(fill = pmax(change_pct, -0.6), size = pred_now), shape = 21, colour = "white", stroke = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(d, new), aes(colour = line_new), shape = 18, size = 2.4) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c(PAL$loss, "#D88C74", PAL$loss_lt, "#B9BEC6"), limits = c(-0.6, 0.05),
                       labels = label_percent(), name = "Change in boardings") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(JRL = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], CRL = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), name = "New station") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 5, guide = "none") +
  sg_crop(stations) + theme_map()
code 
res |> filter(existing) |> arrange(change) |> head(10) |>
  transmute(Station = name, `Lines today` = lines_now, `Today (model)` = num(pred_now, 100),
            `2030 (model)` = num(pred_2030, 100), Change = pct(change_pct),
            `95% interval of change` = paste(num(change_lo, 100), "to", num(change_hi, 100))) |>
  kable()

The losses are concentrated where the new lines run between existing stations rather than beyond them. In the west, the JRL’s Jurong West branch (Gek Poh, Bahar Junction, Corporation, Jurong West) takes the estates that today walk or ride to Chinese Garden, Lakeside, Pioneer and Boon Lay, and the Tengah stations take riders from Bukit Batok and Bukit Gombak. In the north-east the CRL’s Serangoon North and Tavistock draw from Kovan and Serangoon. For the operator this is relief rather than loss: these are among the busiest morning stations on the East-West and North-South lines, and riders who board the JRL at home still join the East-West Line at Jurong East and Boon Lay, now further along their journey.

7.3 Market areas

code 
west <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(c(xmin = 11000, xmax = 23500, ymin = 31000, ymax = 42500), crs = st_crs(STUDY_CRS)))
o_w <- origins |> st_filter(west) |> left_join(scn$dom, by = "origin_id")
top <- union(names(sort(table(o_w$station_now), decreasing = TRUE))[1:12], names(sort(table(o_w$station_2030), decreasing = TRUE))[1:14])
pal_st <- setNames(rep_len(c("#137C8B", "#B4432F", "#5E7CA4", "#C9913D", "#4E8F5A", "#8A5A8C", "#2F6F86", "#C76B4F",
                             "#7A8F3C", "#9C6B3F", "#3E7F72", "#A2546C", "#5C6C99", "#B08A2E", "#6F5A9A", "#3F8A5C"), length(top)), top)
stn_w <- st_filter(lines_sf(stations), west)
o_w <- o_w |> mutate(change = case_when(to_new ~ "Switches to a new station",
                                       switched ~ "Switches to another existing station",
                                       TRUE ~ "Keeps its station"))
p_now <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = st_crop(subzone, west), fill = PAL$land, colour = PAL$land_line, linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = o_w, aes(colour = ifelse(station_now %in% top, station_now, "other")), size = 0.8) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(stn_w, existing), shape = 21, size = 1.8, colour = PAL$ink, fill = "white") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal_st, other = PAL$null), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Today") + theme_map() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
p_30 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = st_crop(subzone, west), fill = PAL$land, colour = PAL$land_line, linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = o_w, aes(colour = change), size = 0.8) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(stn_w, existing), shape = 21, size = 1.8, colour = PAL$ink, fill = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = filter(stn_w, !existing), aes(fill = kind), shape = 23, size = 2.4, colour = PAL$ink) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Switches to a new station" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]],
                                 "Switches to another existing station" = PAL$loss,
                                 "Keeps its station" = PAL$null), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Jurong Region Line" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], "Cross Island Line" = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), guide = "none") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
  labs(title = "2030, with the JRL") + theme_map() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
(p_now + p_30) & theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA))

Across the island, 1,342 of the 10,817 blocks change their dominant station in 2030, and 1,042 of them switch to a new station. The west changes most: Tengah’s blocks, which today split between Bukit Batok and Choa Chu Kang at the edge of both catchments, get stations of their own, and the Jurong West estates divide among four JRL stations.

8 Value-added analysis: does distance decay differ across Singapore?

The chosen model uses one distance exponent for the whole island, and its residuals are spatially autocorrelated. That is the same assumption Lessons 9 and 10 relaxed for regression with GWR: a single parameter says a resident of Punggol and one of Bukit Merah trade distance against station quality in the same way. Feeder bus networks, estate layouts and the walking environment differ across the island, so the decay may too. I fitted two extensions of M3 and scored them with the same cross-validation folds:

  • R5, with one distance exponent per region of the origin block, five in all;
  • EXP, with exponential rather than power decay, the usual alternative form.
code 
p1 <- ggplot(lr, aes(lambda, reorder(region, lambda))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = th[["lambda"]], linetype = 2, colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL$accent, size = 2.4) +
  labs(x = "Distance exponent", y = NULL) + theme_ex03(grid = "x")
p2 <- ggplot(cv_va, aes(R2_log, reorder(model, R2_log))) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL$accent_lt, width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", R2_log)), hjust = 1.1, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink) +
  labs(x = "Cross-validated R² (log boardings)", y = NULL) + theme_ex03(grid = "x")
p1 + p2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1.1, 1))

Two things come out of it.

Distance decay is not uniform. Residents of the North-East (-4.11, interval -5.5 to -2.3) and the West (-3.81, -5.3 to -2.3) are about twice as sensitive to distance as residents of the Central region (-1.84, -2.4 to -1.4), and the intervals barely touch. A likely reason is how the towns are built. In Sengkang, Punggol, Jurong West or Choa Chu Kang, each neighbourhood is laid out around its own MRT or LRT stop, and residents board at the nearest one. In Toa Payoh, Bishan or Queenstown several stations lie within a short walk, and residents pass the nearest to reach a better connected one, which a flatter decay describes. The East and North estimates are too uncertain to read: their intervals span almost any plausible value.

The regional model predicts better, and not only in-sample. Its cross-validated R² is 0.774 against 0.747 for the single exponent, and its median miss falls from 34.4% to 31.5%. It reduces the spatial clustering of the residuals (Moran’s I from 0.16 to 0.12) without removing it, which fits the earlier diagnosis that unseen private housing is the larger cause. Exponential decay is worse than the power form (0.681), so the power function stays.

Do the 2030 conclusions survive it? The JRL runs through the West, where the regional exponent is far steeper than the island-wide one, so I re-ran the scenario with the regional model (R/07_scenario_r5.R). The ranking of the 30 new stations barely moves (Spearman 0.95), predicted JRL boardings rise by 4% in total and CRL boardings fall by 4%, and the same stations sit at the bottom. The changes at existing stations rank almost identically (Spearman 0.96). The one material difference is where the decay matters most: Jurong East’s loss deepens from 33% to 58% and Boon Lay’s from 32% to 45%, because western residents give up a farther interchange more readily once a JRL station opens nearer home. That strengthens, rather than changes, the case that the JRL relieves the western end of the East-West Line.

The value-added analysis therefore does two jobs. It shows that the distance-decay assumption is a geographical one that varies across Singapore in an interpretable way, and it shows that the planning conclusions do not depend on getting that assumption right, except at the western interchanges, where the regional model is the better guide.

9 Implications for transport planning

The brief asks for public-safety and peace-keeping implications, a carry-over from Take-home Exercise 2 that does not fit a question about rail ridership. The implications here are for the planners and operators who decide when a station opens and how a line is run.

Open the residential JRL stations with the line, and plan for their crowds. Tengah Plantation, Choa Chu Kang West and the Jurong West branch stations are predicted to board as many people in the morning peak as busy existing heartland stations do today. They should not be candidates for a delayed opening.

Treat the destination stations as a different kind of investment. Aviation Park, Jurong Pier, Jurong Hill and Loyang draw almost nobody from home in the morning. If their opening is to be judged, it should be judged on the employment and development around them, measured as morning tap-outs, and timed to it. That is the Hume and Buangkok decision, and this model gives the residential half of the evidence for it.

Expect relief on the East-West Line’s western end. The model moves 40% to 65% of the home-based morning boardings at Chinese Garden, Lakeside and Pioneer to the JRL. Feeder bus routes in Jurong West and Bukit Batok built around those stations will need to be redrawn towards the new ones.

Use the model before a station’s opening date is set. The cross-validation is the test that matters here: with a station’s location and attributes, and no knowledge of its ridership, the model predicts its morning boardings with a median error of about a third and ranks it correctly against the others.

10 Limitations

The model sees only HDB residents. Private housing, which accounts for about one resident in five, is invisible to it, which is why stations in private estates were left out of the fit and why the impact estimates for stations near large condominium clusters (Serangoon North, Tavistock) are likely understated.

It predicts home-based morning boardings, not total ridership. A station built for jobs, schools or an airport terminal will look weak here and may still be busy. A full model would add the destination side, using morning tap-outs or the origin-destination data, with employment as the attraction.

Straight-line distance stands in for the walking and feeder-bus journey. Expressways, rivers and the layout of estates make some stations further than they look.

Attributes of the new stations are measured on today’s built environment. Bus stops, shops and services around a station in Tengah or the Jurong Innovation District will change by 2030; the predictions for those stations are a floor, not a forecast of the mature station.

Population is held at today’s. New blocks completing between now and 2030 in Tengah, Bayshore and elsewhere are not in the HDB file yet.

Three months of data from one year: the model describes the network of late 2026, and its parameters may drift as working patterns change.

  • Wieland, T. (2017). Market area analysis for retail and service locations with MCI. The R Journal, 9(1), 298-323.
  • Zhu, Z. et al. (2021). Improved Huff model for estimating urban rail transit station catchment areas considering station choices. Journal of Advanced Transportation, 2021.
  • Lin, T. G., Xia, J. C., Robinson, T. P. et al. (2016). Enhanced Huff model for estimating Park and Ride (PnR) catchment areas in Perth, WA. Journal of Transport Geography, 54, 336-348.

# Introduction and study context

Singapore's rail network is planned decades ahead of the people who will ride it.
The Land Transport Authority builds stations as shells where housing is expected,
and opens them when the riders arrive. Sometimes they arrive late. Hume station on
the Downtown Line had its structure finished in 2015 and opened on 28 February 2025,
a decade later. Buangkok and Woodleigh stayed dark when the North East Line opened
in 2003, because the operator judged that the riders around them would not cover
the cost of stopping there. Several shells are still dark today: the station layer
LTA publishes in September 2026 contains platforms at Bukit Brown, Mount Pleasant,
Marina South and Founders' Memorial that carry no passengers at all (section 4.2).

Two lines now under construction add more than thirty stations by 2030: the Jurong
Region Line (JRL) in the west, serving Tengah, Jurong West and the Jurong
Innovation District, and phase 1 of the Cross Island Line (CRL) from Aviation Park
to Bright Hill. The questions a planner would ask are the ones this exercise asks:
how many people will board at each new station, and which existing stations will
lose riders to them.

These are questions about catchments, and a catchment is a probabilistic thing.
A block of flats between two stations does not belong to either; some of its
residents walk to one and some to the other, in proportions that depend on how far
each station is and how much each offers. That is precisely what a Huff model
describes, and why I use one.

# Research question and objectives

**Where do HDB residents board the train in the morning peak, and how will the
Jurong Region Line and the Cross Island Line phase 1 redistribute them?**

1. Calibrate a probabilistic spatial interaction (Huff) model that estimates
   station-level morning boardings from where people live, how far each station is,
   and what each station offers, and test it against simpler reference models.
2. Use it to predict morning boardings at the planned JRL and CRL phase 1 stations,
   with uncertainty.
3. Show how the new stations change the boardings and market areas of the stations
   already open.

# Data and study design

## What is modelled

The brief asks for station-level ridership. I model one specific part of it: **tap-ins
on weekday mornings between 6:00 and 9:00**, averaged over August, September and
October 2026. The choice is deliberate. A Huff model of station catchments needs the
riders it allocates to come from the places it allocates them from. In the morning
peak most trips begin at home, so a station's boardings are drawn from the housing
around it. Over the whole day that stops being true: a station in the central area
boards thousands of people in the evening who live nowhere near it. Figure 1 shows the
difference in the data itself.

The local market potential of each origin is the number of HDB dwelling units in
it. HDB flats house about four in five Singapore residents, and they are the only
housing for which a public, block-level count exists. Private housing is the main
omission, and it decides which stations the model can be judged on (section 4.3).

## Data sources

| Data | Source | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Passenger Volume by Train Stations, Aug to Oct 2026 | LTA DataMall API (`PV/Train`) | observed tap-ins per station, hour and day type |
| Train Station (Sep 2026) | LTA DataMall static data | checking which stations exist and operate |
| Station coordinates, operational and planned | elliotwutingfeng/singapore_train_station_coordinates (URA data via data.gov.sg), pinned to commit `9f5972c` | station locations and codes, including JRL and CRL |
| HDB Property Information | data.gov.sg | dwelling units per block |
| HDB Existing Building | data.gov.sg | block footprints |
| Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary | data.gov.sg (URA) | regions and planning areas, map underlay |
| OpenStreetMap, Malaysia-Singapore-Brunei extract | Geofabrik | points of interest and bus stops around each station |
| OneMap search API | Singapore Land Authority | geocoding, to link the two HDB files |

: Data used. Every file is fetched by `R/00_download.R` except the LTA static file, which LTA's server will only release to a browser. {#tbl-data}

The brief recommends the origin-destination version of the passenger data. On the day
I ran the analysis DataMall refused that endpoint for my key with a quota violation,
while the station-level endpoint answered normally. For a model of where people
board, station-level tap-ins are all that is needed: the destination half of each
trip plays no part in it. LTA's bus stop file likewise could not be fetched by
script, and OpenStreetMap supplies 5,668 bus stops in its place.


# Data preparation and quality assessment

## Placing every HDB block

The dwelling-unit counts and the building footprints come in two files that share no
key. The property file names a block by number and abbreviated street ("1 BEDOK STH
AVE 1"); the footprint file by number and a street code ("BEA09N") and postal code.
Matching on block number alone is wrong, because block numbers repeat across streets
and towns. The street code turns out to be one code per street (657 street names,
660 codes), so geocoding one block per street with the OneMap search API, and
matching the returned postal code to a footprint, gives a complete street-to-code
crosswalk (`R/01_street_codes.R`). That joins 10,734 of the 10,817 residential
blocks. The other 83, mostly new blocks in Tengah built after the footprint file was
last updated, were geocoded one by one and kept as points. Every residential block,
and all `r num(sum(origins$du))` dwelling units, is placed. Each block's origin point
is a point on the surface of its footprint (`st_point_on_surface()`, in SVY21,
EPSG:3414), which unlike a centroid always falls inside an L-shaped or U-shaped block.

```{r fig-origins}
#| fig-cap: "The local market potential: 10,817 HDB residential blocks sized by dwelling units, with today's stations and the 30 planned JRL and CRL phase 1 stations."
#| fig-height: 5.6
s_all <- lines_sf(stations)
ggplot() + base_land(subzone) +
  geom_sf(data = origins, aes(size = du), colour = PAL$muted, alpha = 0.25, stroke = 0) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(s_all, kind == "Existing"), shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = PAL$ink, size = 1.1, stroke = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(s_all, kind != "Existing"), aes(fill = kind), shape = 21, colour = "white", size = 2.3, stroke = 0.4) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 1.6, guide = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Jurong Region Line" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], "Cross Island Line" = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(caption = "HDB Property Information and Existing Building (data.gov.sg); station coordinates from URA via data.gov.sg.") +
  sg_crop(stations) + theme_map()
```

## Stations: what the passenger data says exists

A station appears in this analysis as a *complex*: Jurong East is one place to a
resident walking from home, whether it serves one line or three. Codes were grouped
by station name, giving `r sum(stations$existing)` existing complexes and
`r sum(stations$new)` new ones (`r sum(str_detect(newS$lines_2030, "JRL"))` on the JRL,
`r sum(str_detect(newS$lines_2030, "CRL"))` on the CRL phase 1). Seven existing stations
gain a line in 2030 (Ang Mo Kio, Boon Lay, Bright Hill, Choa Chu Kang, Hougang,
Jurong East and Pasir Ris), and the model counts their extra line only in the 2030
run.

The passenger data, not any station list, decides what operates. Three mines had
to be cleared here:

- **Stations listed as planned that are already open.** Keppel, Cantonment and
  Prince Edward Road, Circle Line stage 6, appear in the station list as future
  stations but carry passengers in all three months. They are moved to the existing
  network, as are the new Circle Line codes at Marina Bay (CC33) and Bayfront (CC34).
- **Stations that are built but not open.** LTA's own September 2026 station layer
  contains platform polygons for Bukit Brown (CC18), Mount Pleasant (TE10), Marina
  South (TE21) and Founders' Memorial (TE22A), and a dozen depots, none of which
  board a single passenger. Taking that layer as the network would have added the
  very ghost stations the brief describes.
- **Joint codes.** The passenger data codes an interchange once ("NS27/CC33/TE20"),
  so each data code is mapped to the complex of whichever of its parts the station
  list knows.

Morning boardings are stable from month to month: the correlation of log tap-ins
between August and October is `r round(mon_cor[1, 3], 3)`. Averaging the three months
removes the effect of any single month's disruption without hiding real differences.

## Which stations the model can be judged on

`r sum(ex$du_1km < CAL_MIN_DU_1KM)` existing stations have fewer than 1,000 HDB dwelling
units within 1 km. Some serve private estates (Newton, Stevens, Sixth Avenue,
Siglap, Hillview), some industry (Tuas, Joo Koon) or the airport, some the central
area. Newton and Kranji each board more than 200,000 people a month in the morning
peak with no HDB block within a kilometre. A model whose market potential is HDB
flats cannot explain them, and fitting to them would bend every parameter towards
explaining riders it has no data on.

So the rule (set in `R/00_config.R`) is that these stations stay in every block's
choice set, where they compete for HDB riders like any other station, but their
observed boardings do not enter the fit. Figure 1 supports the rule from the data:
the `r n_fit` fitted stations board `r round(with(st_drop_geometry(stn)[cal$cal_idx, ], sum(tap_am) / sum(tapout_am)), 2)`
morning tap-ins for every tap-out; the excluded ones only
`r round(with(st_drop_geometry(stn)[-cal$cal_idx, ], sum(tap_am) / sum(tapout_am)), 2)`.

## Attraction variables

Each station's attractiveness is measured within 400 m of it, about a five-minute
walk:

- **Lines served** today (and in 2030 for the scenario). A second line multiplies
  the destinations reachable without a transfer.
- **Bus stops**, as a measure of feeder connectivity.
- **Points of interest**: shops, food outlets, offices, schools, clinics and civic
  amenities in OpenStreetMap. Mapped areas (many malls and schools are drawn as
  outlines) are reduced to a point on their surface.
- **LRT-only**: whether the station is served only by a light rail loop, from which
  most journeys continue by transferring to the MRT.

Counts enter as log(1 + count), so their exponents read as elasticities.

# Methods and analytical decisions

## The Huff model

The probability that a resident of block $i$ boards at station $j$ is

$$
P_{ij} = \frac{A_j \, d_{ij}^{\lambda}}{\sum_{l \in C_i} A_l \, d_{il}^{\lambda}},
\qquad
A_j = \exp\Big(\sum_m \gamma_m x_{jm}\Big)
$$

where $d_{ij}$ is the straight-line distance from the block to the station, $C_i$ is
the block's choice set and $A_j$ is the station's attractiveness, multiplicative in
its characteristics $x_{jm}$ as in an MCI model. The predicted boardings at station $j$
are the dwelling units allocated to it, scaled by one trip rate $k$:

$$
\hat T_j = k \sum_i DU_i \, P_{ij}
$$

Three decisions shape it.

**Choice set.** A block chooses among the stations within 3 km, and always among its
three nearest, so that blocks far from the network (Tengah has no station today)
still choose. 3 km covers a walk and a short feeder-bus ride; it gives a median of
ten candidate stations per block.

**Distance floor.** Distances under 100 m are set to 100 m, so that a block beside
a station does not receive an effectively infinite pull under a power decay.

**Calibration.** The parameters ($\lambda$ and the $\gamma_m$) minimise the mean squared
error of *log* boardings across the fitted stations, with $k$ solved in closed form.
Boardings range from under a thousand to over 400,000 a month, and on the log scale
a 20% miss costs the same at a small station as at a large one. Because the utility
is linear in the parameters, the Huff model is a conditional logit over stations and
the loss has an exact gradient (`R/huff_core.R`), which makes a 200-draw bootstrap
practical.

The shares are checked against `MCI::huff.shares()` for one block: they agree to the
15th decimal place (largest difference `r sprintf("%.1e", cal$mci_check)`), which is
floating-point noise. The MCI function
needs every origin to share one set of stations, which is why the fitting uses a
vectorised version; MCI is the reference it is checked against.

## Reference models and validation

The rubric asks for reference and null models, and they are the only way to know
whether the attraction terms earn their place. Four nested models are compared:

| Model | Attractiveness | Distance exponent |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | every station equal | -2, the textbook default, not fitted |
| M1 | every station equal | fitted |
| M2 | lines served | fitted |
| M3 | lines, bus stops, points of interest, LRT-only | fitted |

: The four models. {#tbl-models}

Each is scored by **10-fold cross-validation over stations**: a tenth of the stations
have their boardings hidden, the model is fitted on the rest, and the hidden
stations are predicted. The hidden stations stay in every choice set. This is
exactly the position of a new station, whose location and attributes are known and
whose ridership is not, so the cross-validated error is the honest estimate of how
well the model will predict the JRL and CRL stations.

# Calibration results

## Attraction matters more than distance

```{r tbl-fit}
#| tbl-cap: "Fit across the 148 stations with an HDB catchment. R² and RMSLE are on log boardings; MdAPE is the median absolute percentage error."
bind_rows(cal$insample |> mutate(score = "In-sample"), cal$cv |> mutate(score = "Cross-validated")) |>
  select(model, score, R2_log, RMSLE, MdAPE_pct, spearman) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = score, values_from = c(R2_log, RMSLE, MdAPE_pct, spearman)) |>
  transmute(Model = model,
            `R² in-sample` = round(`R2_log_In-sample`, 3), `R² cross-validated` = round(`R2_log_Cross-validated`, 3),
            `RMSLE (CV)` = round(`RMSLE_Cross-validated`, 3), `MdAPE % (CV)` = round(`MdAPE_pct_Cross-validated`, 1),
            `Spearman (CV)` = round(`spearman_Cross-validated`, 3)) |>
  kable()
```

The textbook model already explains `r pct(cv_of("M0", "R2_log"))` of the variation in log
boardings: where the housing is accounts for a good deal. Fitting the distance exponent
alone adds nothing (`r round(cal$fits$M1$theta[["lambda"]], 2)` against the default -2).
Adding the number of lines lifts the cross-validated R² to `r pct(cv_of("M2", "R2_log"))`,
and the full model to `r pct(cv_of("M3", "R2_log"))`, with a median miss of
`r round(cv_of("M3", "MdAPE_pct"))`% and a rank correlation of `r round(cv_of("M3", "spearman"), 2)`.
The cross-validated scores sit close to the in-sample ones, so the extra terms are
not fitting noise.

```{r fig-params}
#| fig-cap: "Estimated parameters of the chosen model (M3) with 95% bootstrap intervals from 200 resamples of the fitted stations."
#| fig-height: 3.2
lab_terms <- c(lambda = "Distance exponent (lambda)", n_lines = "Lines served", bus_stops = "Bus stops within 400 m",
               poi = "Points of interest within 400 m", lrt_only = "LRT-only station")
p <- tibble(term = names(th), estimate = th) |> left_join(cal$ci, by = "term") |>
  mutate(term = factor(lab_terms[term], rev(lab_terms)))
ggplot(p, aes(estimate, term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL$accent, size = 2.4) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", estimate)), vjust = -0.9, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink) +
  labs(x = "Estimate (exponent on log(1 + count); coefficient on the LRT indicator)", y = NULL) +
  theme_ex03(grid = "x")
```

Read as elasticities, the estimates say four things.

- **Distance decays steeply.** $\lambda$ = `r round(th[["lambda"]], 2)`
  (`r round(cal$ci$lo[cal$ci$term == "lambda"], 2)` to `r round(cal$ci$hi[cal$ci$term == "lambda"], 2)`):
  doubling the distance to a station cuts its pull by a factor of
  `r round(2^-th[["lambda"]], 1)`, once its attractions are accounted for. The textbook -2 is
  inside the interval, but with the attractions in the model the data prefer a
  slightly steeper decay.
- **Lines served is the strongest attraction.** Going from one line to two multiplies a
  station's pull by `r round((3/2)^th[["n_lines"]], 1)`. People walk further to an
  interchange because it saves them a transfer later.
- **Activity around the station adds a smaller pull.** Ten times the points of interest
  multiplies attractiveness by `r round(10^th[["poi"]], 2)`.
- **LRT-only stations draw far fewer boardings.** An LRT-only station has
  `r pct(exp(th[["lrt_only"]]))` of the attractiveness of an MRT station with the same
  attributes. Much of that is how LRT riders appear in the data: a Punggol resident
  who boards the LRT and transfers to the North East Line taps in once.

Bus stops, once the other terms are in, are not distinguishable from zero (the interval
spans zero). Feeder connectivity is real, but around stations it moves with lines and
activity, which carry the information.

## Where the model misses

```{r fig-obs-pred}
#| fig-cap: "Observed against cross-validated predicted boardings for the 148 fitted stations. Labelled: the ten largest misses."
#| fig-height: 5.2
d <- st_drop_geometry(stn)[cal$cal_idx, ] |> mutate(cv = cal$cv_pred[[cal$best]][cal$cal_idx], err = log(tap_am / cv))
lab <- d |> slice_max(abs(err), n = 10)
ggplot(d, aes(cv, tap_am)) +
  geom_abline(colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.3, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = lrt_only), size = 1.9, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(data = lab, aes(label = name), size = 2.8, colour = PAL$ink, seed = 2, min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) + scale_y_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = PAL$accent, `TRUE` = LINE_COLS[["LRT"]]),
                      labels = c(`FALSE` = "MRT", `TRUE` = "LRT only"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Predicted (held out in cross-validation), per month", y = "Observed tap-ins, weekday 06:00 to 09:00, per month") +
  theme_ex03(grid = "both")
```

```{r fig-resid-map}
#| fig-cap: "Log residual (observed over predicted) of the chosen model at each fitted station. Teal: the model under-predicts; red: it over-predicts."
#| fig-height: 5
d <- stn[cal$cal_idx, ]
ggplot() + base_land(subzone) +
  geom_sf(data = d, aes(fill = pmax(pmin(resid_log, 1.2), -1.2)), shape = 21, size = 2.4, colour = "white", stroke = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$div, limits = c(-1.2, 1.2), name = "log(observed / predicted)") +
  sg_crop(stations) + theme_map()
```

The residuals are not random in space: Moran's I is
`r round(cal$moran_resid$estimate[1], 2)` (p `r format.pval(cal$moran_resid$p.value, digits = 2)`)
with six nearest neighbours. The largest under-predictions are city-fringe stations
whose catchments mix HDB blocks with condominiums and landed housing: Novena, Great
World, Katong Park, Fort Canning, Beauty World, Aljunied. Their extra boardings come
from residents the model cannot see. The largest over-predictions are of two kinds:
stations that opened recently, where habits have not caught up (Keppel, in service
only since 2026, and the small Punggol LRT stop at Teck Lee), and stations whose HDB
blocks mostly walk to a stronger neighbour, such as Bendemeer, Labrador Park and
one-north. Both patterns are regional, which is what Moran's I picks up. Private
housing cannot be added from the data available, but a single distance exponent for
the whole island is a testable suspect, and section 8 tests it.

# Predicting the 2030 network

The calibrated model is run twice on the same 10,817 blocks: on today's stations and on
the 2030 set, in which the 30 new stations exist and seven interchanges count their
extra line. Comparing two runs of the same model isolates the effect of the new
stations; comparing a prediction with observed ridership would mix that effect with the
model's own error. The intervals come from re-running the 200 bootstrap draws of the
parameters through both networks.

## Ridership at the new stations

```{r fig-new}
#| fig-cap: "Predicted weekday morning-peak boardings per month at the 30 new stations, with 95% bootstrap intervals. The grey band is the range of today's fitted stations between their 10th and 50th percentiles."
#| fig-height: 7
q <- quantile(stn$tap_am[cal$cal_idx], c(0.1, 0.5))
d <- res |> filter(new) |> mutate(name = reorder(name, pred_2030),
                                 line = ifelse(line_new == "JRL", "Jurong Region Line", "Cross Island Line"))
ggplot(d, aes(pred_2030, name)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = q[1], xmax = q[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = PAL$land, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = pred_2030_lo, xmax = pred_2030_hi, colour = line), height = 0, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = line), size = 2.2) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Jurong Region Line" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], "Cross Island Line" = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Predicted boardings per month, weekday 06:00 to 09:00 (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_ex03(grid = "x")
```

```{r new-numbers}
#| include: false
nn <- res |> filter(new) |> arrange(-pred_2030)
low <- nn |> filter(pred_2030 < q[1])
```

The strongest new stations are those planted in dense housing with no station of
its own today. Tengah Plantation (`r num(nn$pred_2030[nn$name == "Tengah Plantation"], 100)` a month)
is the clearest case: Tengah's `r num(sum(origins$du[origins$PLN_AREA_N == "TENGAH"]))`
dwelling units currently have to reach Bukit Batok or Choa Chu Kang. On the CRL,
Serangoon North (`r num(nn$pred_2030[nn$name == "Serangoon North"], 100)`) and Pasir Ris East
(`r num(nn$pred_2030[nn$name == "Pasir Ris East"], 100)`) serve large estates that sit between
today's lines.

`r nrow(low)` new stations fall below the 10th percentile of today's stations:
`r paste(as.character(low$name), collapse = ", ")`. Most are in the Jurong Innovation
District, at the airport or on the edge of Tengah, where there are few or no homes.
In a home-based morning model they are exactly what the brief calls the ghost-station
risk. Two cautions apply. First, their case does not rest on boardings at all: they are
destinations, built for the jobs, campuses and terminal that will arrive, and their
morning ridership will show up as tap-outs, which this model does not predict. Second,
some are in towns still under construction (Tengah, Forest Hill), where today's
points of interest and bus stops understate what the station will offer in 2030.

## What the new stations take from the existing ones

```{r fig-impact}
#| fig-cap: "Change in predicted morning boardings at existing stations when the JRL and CRL phase 1 open (same model, 2030 network against today's). New stations in their line colours."
#| fig-height: 5.6
d <- stations |> select(name) |> left_join(res, by = "name")
ggplot() + base_land(subzone) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(d, existing, !is.na(change_pct)),
          aes(fill = pmax(change_pct, -0.6), size = pred_now), shape = 21, colour = "white", stroke = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(d, new), aes(colour = line_new), shape = 18, size = 2.4) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c(PAL$loss, "#D88C74", PAL$loss_lt, "#B9BEC6"), limits = c(-0.6, 0.05),
                       labels = label_percent(), name = "Change in boardings") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(JRL = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], CRL = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), name = "New station") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 5, guide = "none") +
  sg_crop(stations) + theme_map()
```

```{r tbl-losers}
#| tbl-cap: "The existing stations that lose the most morning boardings, in absolute terms."
res |> filter(existing) |> arrange(change) |> head(10) |>
  transmute(Station = name, `Lines today` = lines_now, `Today (model)` = num(pred_now, 100),
            `2030 (model)` = num(pred_2030, 100), Change = pct(change_pct),
            `95% interval of change` = paste(num(change_lo, 100), "to", num(change_hi, 100))) |>
  kable()
```

The losses are concentrated where the new lines run between existing stations
rather than beyond them. In the west, the JRL's Jurong West branch (Gek Poh, Bahar
Junction, Corporation, Jurong West) takes the estates that today walk or ride to
Chinese Garden, Lakeside, Pioneer and Boon Lay, and the Tengah stations take
riders from Bukit Batok and Bukit Gombak. In the north-east the CRL's Serangoon North
and Tavistock draw from Kovan and Serangoon. For the operator this is relief rather
than loss: these are among the busiest morning stations on the East-West and North-South
lines, and riders who board the JRL at home still join the East-West Line at Jurong
East and Boon Lay, now further along their journey.

## Market areas

```{r fig-market}
#| fig-cap: "Market areas in the west. Left: each HDB block coloured by the station that draws the largest share of its residents today. Right: the blocks whose main station changes when the JRL opens, and whether they move to a new station or to another existing one."
#| fig-height: 5.4
west <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(c(xmin = 11000, xmax = 23500, ymin = 31000, ymax = 42500), crs = st_crs(STUDY_CRS)))
o_w <- origins |> st_filter(west) |> left_join(scn$dom, by = "origin_id")
top <- union(names(sort(table(o_w$station_now), decreasing = TRUE))[1:12], names(sort(table(o_w$station_2030), decreasing = TRUE))[1:14])
pal_st <- setNames(rep_len(c("#137C8B", "#B4432F", "#5E7CA4", "#C9913D", "#4E8F5A", "#8A5A8C", "#2F6F86", "#C76B4F",
                             "#7A8F3C", "#9C6B3F", "#3E7F72", "#A2546C", "#5C6C99", "#B08A2E", "#6F5A9A", "#3F8A5C"), length(top)), top)
stn_w <- st_filter(lines_sf(stations), west)
o_w <- o_w |> mutate(change = case_when(to_new ~ "Switches to a new station",
                                       switched ~ "Switches to another existing station",
                                       TRUE ~ "Keeps its station"))
p_now <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = st_crop(subzone, west), fill = PAL$land, colour = PAL$land_line, linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = o_w, aes(colour = ifelse(station_now %in% top, station_now, "other")), size = 0.8) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(stn_w, existing), shape = 21, size = 1.8, colour = PAL$ink, fill = "white") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal_st, other = PAL$null), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Today") + theme_map() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
p_30 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = st_crop(subzone, west), fill = PAL$land, colour = PAL$land_line, linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = o_w, aes(colour = change), size = 0.8) +
  geom_sf(data = filter(stn_w, existing), shape = 21, size = 1.8, colour = PAL$ink, fill = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = filter(stn_w, !existing), aes(fill = kind), shape = 23, size = 2.4, colour = PAL$ink) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Switches to a new station" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]],
                                 "Switches to another existing station" = PAL$loss,
                                 "Keeps its station" = PAL$null), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Jurong Region Line" = LINE_COLS[["JRL"]], "Cross Island Line" = LINE_COLS[["CRL"]]), guide = "none") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
  labs(title = "2030, with the JRL") + theme_map() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11))
(p_now + p_30) & theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA))
```

Across the island, `r num(sum(scn$dom$switched))` of the 10,817 blocks change their dominant
station in 2030, and `r num(sum(scn$dom$to_new))` of them switch to a new station. The west
changes most: Tengah's blocks, which today split between Bukit Batok and Choa Chu Kang
at the edge of both catchments, get stations of their own, and the Jurong West estates
divide among four JRL stations.

# Value-added analysis: does distance decay differ across Singapore?

```{r va-numbers}
#| include: false
lr <- va$lambda_region |> mutate(region = str_to_title(sub(" REGION", "", region)))
cv_va <- bind_rows(cal$cv |> filter(model == "M3") |> mutate(model = "M3: one lambda"),
                   va$cv |> mutate(model = recode(model, R5 = "R5: a lambda per region", EXP = "EXP: exponential decay")))
```

The chosen model uses one distance exponent for the whole island, and its residuals
are spatially autocorrelated. That is the same assumption Lessons 9 and 10 relaxed for
regression with GWR: a single parameter says a resident of Punggol and one of Bukit
Merah trade distance against station quality in the same way. Feeder bus networks,
estate layouts and the walking environment differ across the island, so the decay may
too. I fitted two extensions of M3 and scored them with the same cross-validation folds:

- **R5**, with one distance exponent per region of the origin block, five in all;
- **EXP**, with exponential rather than power decay, the usual alternative form.

```{r fig-va}
#| fig-cap: "Left: distance exponent by region of the origin block, with 95% bootstrap intervals (100 resamples); the dashed line is the single island-wide exponent. Right: cross-validated R² of log boardings."
#| fig-height: 3.6
p1 <- ggplot(lr, aes(lambda, reorder(region, lambda))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = th[["lambda"]], linetype = 2, colour = PAL$muted, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL$accent, size = 2.4) +
  labs(x = "Distance exponent", y = NULL) + theme_ex03(grid = "x")
p2 <- ggplot(cv_va, aes(R2_log, reorder(model, R2_log))) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL$accent_lt, width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", R2_log)), hjust = 1.1, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink) +
  labs(x = "Cross-validated R² (log boardings)", y = NULL) + theme_ex03(grid = "x")
p1 + p2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1.1, 1))
```

Two things come out of it.

**Distance decay is not uniform.** Residents of the North-East
(`r round(lr$lambda[lr$region == "North-East"], 2)`, interval `r round(lr$lo[lr$region == "North-East"], 1)` to
`r round(lr$hi[lr$region == "North-East"], 1)`) and the West (`r round(lr$lambda[lr$region == "West"], 2)`,
`r round(lr$lo[lr$region == "West"], 1)` to `r round(lr$hi[lr$region == "West"], 1)`) are about twice as sensitive to
distance as residents of the Central region (`r round(lr$lambda[lr$region == "Central"], 2)`,
`r round(lr$lo[lr$region == "Central"], 1)` to `r round(lr$hi[lr$region == "Central"], 1)`), and the intervals barely
touch. A likely reason is how the towns are built. In Sengkang, Punggol, Jurong West or
Choa Chu Kang, each neighbourhood is laid out around its own MRT or LRT stop, and
residents board at the nearest one. In Toa Payoh, Bishan or Queenstown several
stations lie within a short walk, and residents pass the nearest to reach a better
connected one, which a flatter decay describes. The East and North estimates are too
uncertain to read: their intervals span almost any plausible value.

**The regional model predicts better, and not only in-sample.** Its cross-validated R²
is `r round(va$cv$R2_log[va$cv$model == "R5"], 3)` against `r round(cv_of("M3", "R2_log"), 3)` for the single exponent,
and its median miss falls from `r round(cv_of("M3", "MdAPE_pct"), 1)`% to
`r round(va$cv$MdAPE_pct[va$cv$model == "R5"], 1)`%. It reduces the spatial clustering of the
residuals (Moran's I from `r round(cal$moran_resid$estimate[1], 2)` to `r round(va$moran_r5$estimate[1], 2)`)
without removing it, which fits the earlier diagnosis that unseen private housing is the
larger cause. Exponential decay is worse than the power form
(`r round(va$cv$R2_log[va$cv$model == "EXP"], 3)`), so the power function stays.

**Do the 2030 conclusions survive it?** The JRL runs through the West, where the regional
exponent is far steeper than the island-wide one, so I re-ran the scenario with the
regional model (`R/07_scenario_r5.R`). The ranking of the 30 new stations barely moves
(Spearman `r round(r5$summ$rho_new, 2)`), predicted JRL boardings rise by
`r pct(r5$summ$ratio_new_jrl - 1)` in total and CRL boardings fall by `r pct(1 - r5$summ$ratio_new_crl)`, and the same
stations sit at the bottom. The changes at existing stations rank almost identically
(Spearman `r round(r5$summ$rho_change, 2)`). The one material difference is where the decay
matters most: Jurong East's loss deepens from
`r pct(-r5$cmp$change_pct[r5$cmp$name == "Jurong East"])` to `r pct(-r5$cmp$change_pct_r5[r5$cmp$name == "Jurong East"])`
and Boon Lay's from `r pct(-r5$cmp$change_pct[r5$cmp$name == "Boon Lay"])` to
`r pct(-r5$cmp$change_pct_r5[r5$cmp$name == "Boon Lay"])`, because western residents give up a
farther interchange more readily once a JRL station opens nearer home. That strengthens,
rather than changes, the case that the JRL relieves the western end of the East-West
Line.

The value-added analysis therefore does two jobs. It shows that the distance-decay
assumption is a geographical one that varies across Singapore in an interpretable way,
and it shows that the planning conclusions do not depend on getting that assumption
right, except at the western interchanges, where the regional model is the better guide.

# Implications for transport planning

The brief asks for public-safety and peace-keeping implications, a carry-over from
Take-home Exercise 2 that does not fit a question about rail ridership. The
implications here are for the planners and operators who decide when a station opens
and how a line is run.

**Open the residential JRL stations with the line, and plan for their crowds.** Tengah
Plantation, Choa Chu Kang West and the Jurong West branch stations are predicted to
board as many people in the morning peak as busy existing heartland stations do today.
They should not be candidates for a delayed opening.

**Treat the destination stations as a different kind of investment.** Aviation Park,
Jurong Pier, Jurong Hill and Loyang draw almost nobody from home in the morning. If
their opening is to be judged, it should be judged on the employment and development
around them, measured as morning tap-outs, and timed to it. That is the Hume and
Buangkok decision, and this model gives the residential half of the evidence for it.

**Expect relief on the East-West Line's western end.** The model moves 40% to 65% of
the home-based morning boardings at Chinese Garden, Lakeside and Pioneer to the JRL.
Feeder bus routes in Jurong West and Bukit Batok built around those stations will need
to be redrawn towards the new ones.

**Use the model before a station's opening date is set.** The cross-validation is the
test that matters here: with a station's location and attributes, and no knowledge of
its ridership, the model predicts its morning boardings with a median error of about a
third and ranks it correctly against the others.

# Limitations

The model sees only **HDB residents**. Private housing, which accounts for about one
resident in five, is invisible to it, which is why stations in private estates were left
out of the fit and why the impact estimates for stations near large condominium
clusters (Serangoon North, Tavistock) are likely understated.

It predicts **home-based morning boardings**, not total ridership. A station built for
jobs, schools or an airport terminal will look weak here and may still be busy. A full
model would add the destination side, using morning tap-outs or the origin-destination
data, with employment as the attraction.

**Straight-line distance** stands in for the walking and feeder-bus journey. Expressways,
rivers and the layout of estates make some stations further than they look.

**Attributes of the new stations** are measured on today's built environment. Bus stops,
shops and services around a station in Tengah or the Jurong Innovation District will
change by 2030; the predictions for those stations are a floor, not a forecast of the
mature station.

**Population is held at today's.** New blocks completing between now and 2030 in Tengah,
Bayshore and elsewhere are not in the HDB file yet.

**Three months** of data from one year: the model describes the network of late 2026,
and its parameters may drift as working patterns change.
